title: Al-Hasib, the Reckoner
hook: the Reckoner, and the One who is enough
tomorrow: is awe just a polite word for fear?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Muqit, the Nourisher, and the line: nourished. Food for the body, knowledge for the heart. Now, a puzzle about counting.

Someone texts hey. You send back hey!! with two exclamation points, because one felt cold. Small math, all day long: who replied fastest, who used a period, who left you on read. The Qur'an has a verse about exactly that. In Surah An-Nisa: when you're greeted with a greeting, answer with a better one, or at least return it. Fair enough. Then the verse ends somewhere odd. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah taketh count of all things." Why does a verse about saying hello end with God keeping count?
screen: `HEY. HEY!!` → `RETURN A GREETING, OR A BETTER ONE.` → `WHY END ON COUNTING?`

segments.voice: The puzzle opens on today's Name: Al-Hasib. It holds two things that sound like they pull apart. Al-Hasib is the Reckoner, the one who keeps the account, down to a returned hello. And al-Hasib is the one who is enough, who suffices. A few verses earlier, the same surah puts both in one short line: "Allah sufficeth as a Reckoner." So here's the answer. Nothing small goes uncounted: not the greeting, not the kindness nobody noticed. And because nothing is lost, you don't have to keep the books yourself. Your nervous scorekeeping can rest. The friend who never texts first, the shift you covered, the thanks that never came: all of it sits on a ledger kept by Someone who doesn't miscount. The one who counts is enough. That's why the phrase hasbiyallah, Allah is enough for me, belongs at the end of your own careful math, not in place of it. In Surah Al Imran, a group is warned that a great force has gathered against them, and their faith grows instead. Their answer: "Allah is Sufficient for us! Most Excellent is He in whom we trust!" Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abbas says those same words were said by Ibrahim when he was thrown into the fire. Two different moments, the same few words. A careful Reckoner, and enough.
screen: `THE ONE WHO KEEPS THE ACCOUNT.` · `THE ONE WHO IS ENOUGH.` · `HASBIYALLAH, AT THE END OF THE MATH.` · `IBRAHIM IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `HE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Say it out loud, softly, once for each worry you're carrying right now: hasbiyallah, Allah is enough for me. If you don't pray, you can say the English, or simply name each worry and set it down beside you. Notice how each one sounds once it has been said. Then let the breath slow for the sit.
screen: `ONE WORRY, ONE HASBIYALLAH.` · `SET IT DOWN.` · `BREATHE SLOW.`

segments.voice: Al-Hasib. The Reckoner who counts all things, even a returned hello, and the one who is enough. Name forty.
Hold onto this one: he is enough, and the counting is already being done. Forty names in.

howItsDone: Muslims say hasbiyallah (Allah is enough for me) or hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil (3:173) in hard moments, and are taught to return a greeting with one as good or better (4:86).

fork.setup: a friend never says thanks when you hold the door, cover a shift, send the notes. you've started a list in your head. which thought fits Al-Hasib?
options: 'every kindness is counted already. i can stop keeping score.'
'God keeps count too, so my list proves i'm right.'
'if nobody notices it, it doesn't really count.'
fork.reveal: the Reckoner counts even a returned hello, so nothing good is lost, and the one who counts is enough. that's what lets you put your own ledger down.

original.note: Arabic: the Reckoner, and the one who suffices. 4:6 puts both in one line: Allah sufficeth as a Reckoner.

trapdoor: what you thought: God the accountant, keeping a list on you.
what it means: the one who counts everything, so nothing good is lost, and who is enough for you.
what a scholar hears: al-Hasib touches both reckoning and sufficing; 4:6 joins them, and 3:173 says hasbunallah, Allah is enough for us.
guess: the one who counts all things and is enough
the one who weighs your sins against you
the one who decides who gets rich this year

chat.says: essay's in!! now the cost calculator. even with aid it's a lot. is 'Allah is enough' just giving up?
options: No. Do the math all the way through; hasbiyallah is what you say at the end of it.
Kind of. If Allah is enough, you don't really need to run the numbers.
Only once the numbers work out. Then you can say it and mean it.
chat.meaning: In the verses, the One who counts everything is also enough. Hasbiyallah sits beside the careful math, not in place of it.
